items.title: My Monitor Was Cutting My Download Speed by 75%
items.content:
My Monitor Was Cutting My Download Speed by 75%

2026-11-15 Oscar Molnar 8 min read (1684 words)

# unifi   Somehow I am one of those few very lucky people to have the opportunity of owning a 2.5 gig symmetrical line for my internet. But one day, when I wanted to brag to my equally nerdy friends, shock and horror: 600 Mbps down? Luckily my upload speed was still 2.4 Gbps, so I didn’t lose all my bragging rights, but that’s weird, right? If anything, you’d expect the opposite!

My ISP is pretty cool. It’s run by this one guy (Hey Keith!), and I know I can always message them and they respond promptly, as they did this time. We tried to run through a few debugging steps, they checked on their end, and everything was normal. I tried my work laptop too, same speed.

I didn’t have time for debugging, because I needed to travel 2000 km to the other side of the continent for a family emergency.

But as soon as I got back, I got curious again. What could it be? In retrospect, I now know when it started: when I moved all my connections onto my Studio Display XDR . I wanted to have a one-cable setup, and the monitor offered me that. I’ve had it for half a year now, and I don’t think I’ve ever run a speed test through it. 600 Mbps was more than fast enough for me to never realise I wasn’t getting three quarters of the speed I was paying for 🤦

2026 Studio Display XDR, with everything plugged into it so switching laptops is one cable

UGREEN USB-C to 2.5G Ethernet adapter, plugged into the display

UniFi Dream Router 7, the same one from my WiFi 7 debugging post

Pings to other wired computers during a download would fail 10% of the time over Ethernet through the adapter plugged into my screen, and 0% of the time over Wi-Fi. What made it stranger was that there were no dropped frame errors in macOS’s logs at all. This was the big hint for me: the adapter was dropping them before the computer could know.

I then plugged the adapter straight into my Mac instead of the monitor, and ran an iperf3 server on my UDR 7: 2.3 Gbps. So the cable, the router and the adapter are all fine? What about fast.com? Perfect speeds there too! 2.2 down and 2.3 up when connected straight in. As soon as I connected it to the display, it was back to 600 down again.

So it’s the display, right? Well, I would find out: sort of yes, sort of no, which is why I wanted to write this blog post. I couldn’t find anything online explaining the exact cause, and it’s quite a cool reason.

The adapter uses a Realtek RTL8156B, which on macOS binds to Apple’s generic USB networking driver. But Realtek ship their own driver on their website , so I thought I’d give that a go! I installed it and, to my surprise, it almost doubled the download speed to 1.1 Gbps, but that was still nowhere close to 2.5. First hint that it couldn’t just be the monitor’s fault.

Then I tried flow control . I had never truly looked into this before, and I think it’s quite neat to know about if you were also ignorant of it like me. Basically, when a device receives Ethernet frames it can’t keep up with, it just drops them. With flow control (it’s something your router or switch has to support), it can send the sender a “pause” frame, and the sender then buffers the data on its side, instead of the receiver (the adapter in this case) on its side. I turned it on in my UniFi console and guess what, download jumped to around 2 Gbps, with upload still at full speed! Yay! Well, not so fast…

I don’t like it always being on, because it can add latency to other systems like my gaming PC. Can you work around it? For sure, you can disable it on those computers, but it’s janky, and it’s another thing I need to remember when my Sauerbraten game starts lagging. I need fewer things to remember, considering I am 30 in a couple of months. My memory is not what it used to be.

Yeah, isn’t that weird? First of all, it looks like the port can indeed do 2.5 in both directions. I already knew that, because I get much more…

items.title: "Dramatic Drop" in Memory Prices Expected by Mid-2027 as Demand Cools and Channel Inventory Gluts Slow New Orders, Says Korean Financial Firm
items.content:
“Dramatic Drop” in Memory Prices Expected by Mid-2027 as Demand Cools and Channel Inventory Gluts Slow New Orders, Says Korean Financial Firm

Most of 2026 went by with inflated prices for DDR5 memory, SSDs, and GPUs but next year may finally bring relief from gamers and tech companies producing consumer electronics, at least according to one market analysis report on SK Hynix coming out of Seoul, Korea.

BNK Investment & Securities analyst Lee Min-hee shares a detailed report warning end-user memory demand has passed its peak and predicted that by mid-2027 channel inventory corrections are coming. Channel inventory adjustment can trigger “dramatic drop” in memory prices.

In the past week, we have also heard from American financial institutions claiming a 20% drop in NAND . Hence, GPUs, phones, laptops, RAM etc. may get cheaper in the next 12 to 18 months, according to multiple reports.

As a result, BNK slashed its six-month target price on South Korean memory giant SK hynix (KRX: 000660) by 36.4%, from 1,650,000 KRW down to 1,050,000 KRW ($780 USD), placing its valuation target below SK hynix’s prior closing price of 1,113,000 KRW ($830 USD) while maintaining a “Hold” rating.

More striking still, BNK’s financial model forecasts SK hynix’s operating profit to plunge 89.0% in 2028 (alongside an 85.9% drop in earnings per share) once the current AI-fueled memory cycle reverses .

Despite memory giant SK Hynix posting record profits this year, BNK notes that final demand momentum has already crested so profit margins cannot be sustained anymore. Moreover, downward hardware makers have hit a cost wall causing consumers hardware sales to drop significantly. Due to rising memory costs, PC and smartphone makers scaled back memory capacities, delayed orders, or passed the price hike down to consumers. Thus, causing a lot of damage to consumer hardware demand.

BNK expects distributors and hardware makers to clear inventory by Q3 2027, slowing down new orders and driving down prices.

This year, DRAM bit demand growth is expected to be 24% year-on-year, while suppliers’ shipment growth is forecast at 38%, which would be the highest since 2016. in line with the consensus that supply shortages will worsen next year, excess inventory seems to be accumulating within the channel.

Excess inventory is a direct cause of the AI mania fueled by Nvidia and its channel stuffing of companies like Google, Meta, Amazon, and a ton of smaller neoclouds; who horded excess RAM and VRAM while data centers weren’t ready. And with the Dems in control next year, Data Centers will have a much harder time to go through.

However, the Democratic Party’s takeover of the U.S. Congress is expected to delay future data center (DC) construction, and as Nvidia’s role as an ‘AI bank’ shrinks following Jensen Huang’s retirement, credit risk for small and mid-sized AI companies will rise and financial institutions will tighten lending. As a result, the related infrastructure investment cycle next year will slow considerably.

Nvidia is already under SEC investigation for alleged financial fraud , and there are reports of incoming investigations into the company’s GPU shipments to China through Megaspeed and its regional subsidiaries. Nvidia’s circular financing kept the demand high for DRAM but the scheme is now falling apart.

PC DRAM and NAND flash are the most sensitive to gluts and if OEMs start to clear their inventory next year, prices are expected to drop; meaning cheaper DDR5 kits, NVMs, and SSDs for retail consumers… an absolute nightmare for Sam Altman .

items.title: C++26 is done (again)! — Trip report: November 2026 ISO C++ standards meeting (Búzios, Brazil)
items.content:
C++26 technical work, originally completed in March, was reopened and is now recompleted: The anticipated plan is to reissue the updated C++26 document for a second approval ballot.

Most of the six-day meeting was devoted to addressing a second set of international comments for C++26, primarily on the contracts language feature.

Adopted this week for draft C++29: break label; continue label; , std::ranges::any_view , views::slice , and more…

Today, the ISO C++ committee completed technical work on C++26 for a second time in beautiful Búzios, Rio de Janeiro, Brazil (hybrid online via Zoom).

As I reported in March , the ISO C++ committee completed technical work on C++26 at our March meeting; following that, we held the first meeting of C++29 in June . Since then, the approval (Draft International Standard, or DIS) ballot for C++26 was held but, for the first time, did not pass unanimously and was sent back to the ISO C++ committee with additional international comments to address, mostly about the contracts feature ( pre , post , and contract_assert ). So this week we addressed the additional comments on C++26, including by adopting an extension to contracts and providing a detailed rationale and timeline to inform national bodies of the history and process by which contracts were developed, concerns heard repeatedly, and decisions made. The committee is now producing an updated final document that is anticipated to be sent out for its second international approval (DIS) ballot and final editorial work, anticipated to be published in the near future by ISO.

This meeting was hosted by C++ Alliance . Thank you to everyone involved and especially to Matheus Izvekov , who took the lead in making the arrangements! Our hosts arranged for high-quality facilities for our six-day meeting from Monday through Saturday. We had about 220 attendees, split about 35%/65% in-person/remote-Zoom, formally representing 27 nations. (The higher-than-usual percentage of remote participation was partly because of the U.S. aviation ground stop that disrupted air travel just as experts were trying to fly to the ISO C++ meeting.) At each meeting we have new guest attendees, and this time there were 13 new guests, mostly in person, in addition to new attendees who are official national body representatives. To all of them, once again welcome!

The committee currently has 22 active subgroups, but this time fewer of them met throughout the week than usual as we focused on the additional C++26 comments.

The most controversial feature in C++26 is contracts: pre , post , and contract_assert . The committee already had strong consensus, and as of the end of this meeting has still stronger consensus, on including the feature in C++26, but we spent most of this meeting rehearing contracts concerns and working hard again to address them.

Here is some history (much of this repeated from my March trip report ): In February 2025, when we took the plenary poll to adopt contracts in the C++26 working draft (“merge it to trunk”), the vote was:

87.7% in favor:opposed — 100 in favor, 14 opposed, and 12 abstaining

After that, the concerns were all deeply rediscussed for the last four meetings of the original C++26 cycle thanks to thoughtful and high-quality technical papers explaining the objections; all of those papers continued to be fully heard, often for multiple days and at many telecons between meetings, with some contracts fixes adopted.

At our meeting in March 2026, when we took the plenary poll to finalize and ship the C++26 standard, the vote was non-unanimous primarily because of the sustained concerns about contracts:

90.5% in favor:opposed — 114 in favor, 12 opposed, and 3 abstaining

As I reported in March: After extensive scrutiny, the ISO C++ committee still wanted C++26 with contracts, and so contracts stayed in C++26 for the ISO DIS ballot.

Our past ISO C++ DIS approval ballots have always been unanimous. No national bodies (NBs) objected to…

items.title: Inkling 2 Mini
items.content:
Today we are releasing Inkling 2 Mini, a fast, powerful model that’s small enough to run on your laptop.

Inkling 2 Mini is a looped transformer, running the middle layers of the model three times for every token. This allows the model to apply more reasoning and reach the right answer with fewer tokens, especially on tasks such as agentic coding that depend on reasoning quality. Inkling 2 Mini leads every open-weights model with less than 100B total parameters on benchmarks such as DeepSWE v1.1 (48.2%) and Vals Index v2.2 (46.5%). It runs faster than similarly performing models as well.

Reported coding scores for models under 100B total parameters. The green line is the frontier with Inkling 2 Mini, the dashed line the frontier without it, and the shading the ground it adds. Decoding speed is a theoretical ceiling at 614 GB/s with BF16 weights and batch size one, including repeated reads across loops. Evaluation setups vary by model.

Inkling 2 Mini is a Mixture-of-Experts model with 26.4B total parameters, 3.4B active, and 5.4B weight activations per token to account for looping. Looping allows the model to reason longer without writing its reasoning down, which matters for monitoring: our ability to oversee and understand what the model does by reading its chain of thought (CoT).

We measured the impact of looping on both performance and monitorability with Inkling 2 Mini and a research-specific variable-loop variant we are releasing alongside it. The variable-loop model’s no-CoT time horizon improved from 16 seconds at one pass to 37 seconds with three, and its performance on a benchmark of serial reasoning kept improving out to ten loops—twice as many as it was trained with. The model’s chain of thought grew shorter with more loops but stayed legible throughout. The model didn’t trend higher on tests of agentic sabotage as loops were added.

We’re excited to offer some of the first models with looped architecture available to researchers. The variable-loop model was used for our monitorability experiments as it allows for cleaner comparisons between different looping depths.

Most of Inkling 2 Mini’s weights were trained and are deployed natively in NVFP4, with the last four layers in MXFP8. The total memory footprint of Inkling 2 Mini is ~20GB, allowing it to run on local devices such as consumer laptops and desktop AI computers. Our researchers took Inkling 2 Mini on a flight, where it ran offline on a MacBook Pro and built a playable flight simulator in a few minutes.

MacBook Pro (M5 Pro, 48GB) Airplane mode

Open video: PlaneBench flight simulator demo, screen with phone video inset

Loading the flight simulator Inkling 2 Mini built… To try the flight simulator, open this page on desktop.

Building and flying a flight simulator with Inkling 2 Mini. The timer shows real time; most of the recording plays at 15× speed.

Inkling 2 Mini is released with open weights and is available on Tinker today for inference and customization.

Inkling 2 Mini’s strengths mirror those of Inkling 2 Small: it does best on long-horizon agentic work and is the best among open-weights models of similar size on most tasks we measured.

Inkling 2 Mini scores ahead of every comparable model on agentic coding benchmarks such as DeepSWE v1.1 and SWE-bench Pro v2, and is behind only Qwen3.8-27B on others. On PMPP-Hard, a kernel-optimization benchmark, it approaches the score of the much larger Inkling 2 Small.

While looping improves the model’s reasoning, it doesn’t enable its weights to store more facts—knowledge is mostly a function of total parameter count. Inkling 2 Mini’s score on AA-Omniscience, a measure of factuality, is in line with other models of the same size. Studying the variable-loop model , we saw that performances on long-context benchmarks improve with more passes, such as GraphWalks BFS and MRCR v2; but knowledge-intensive benchmarks doesn’t improve with more passes, such as AA-Omniscience, SimpleQA Verified, SimpleVQA, and…

items.title: TODOs JJ Style
items.content:
I love using JJ and recently I’ve found a cool way to handle TODOs that works for me.

Usually I’ll put them in a TODO.md file which is pretty standard. But, I forget about this file quickly and am not very good at remembering to cross stuff off. Also since it’s in-tree I’ll often not want to update it, and then forget to do so later.

JJ has a cool feature where you can make empty changes, and even write descriptions for them before actually doing work. So what if I just make all the stuff I wanna do later as empty commits?

Pretty nice! When I want to start working on something I’ll rebase it out of my TODO tree and onto some other change.

I need to rebase my “TODO base” forward when i make changes, but because it’s empty it will never have conflicts and can pretty easily move around.

TODOs that depend on other TODOs also naturally fit here, I just make new empty commits on top of other empty commits.

I have git.private-commits configured to make sure nothing with the private: prefix will get pushed. This ensures my TODOs stay on my local system. Of course, there are benefits to not doing this.

Anyway that’s about it, not very ground breaking but something I like.

items.title: Incident Report: unsanctioned agent behaviour during cyber testing | AISI Work
items.content:
You can access the full technical report here.

AISI’s role is to evaluate and understand the capabilities of frontier AI models, surfacing potential risks before they reach the public. To assess what these models can do, including whether they could be misused for cyberattacks, we test them under deliberately permissive conditions: with access to the open internet, and with some safety filters disabled.

On 28 th July 2026, AISI's Security Team detected unusual data transfers leaving our research systems during a routine cyber evaluation. On investigation, we found that some of the agents being tested had engaged in sustained, potentially harmful activity directed at real people and organisations. We declared a security incident and, within roughly one hour of discovery, had contained it and begun a full investigation.

The incident stemmed from a single evaluation where agents were given a task of solving a cyber security challenge. We ran this challenge 122 times across several models. Our investigation found that in 10 of those runs, an AI agent took autonomous, unsanctioned action on the live internet, targeting real people and organisations. In total, we catalogued 19 such actions. Almost all of this behaviour (17 actions) came from a single model, Anthropic's Mythos 5, with 2 actions involving OpenAI's GPT-5.6-Sol with cyber classifiers (mechanisms to prevent misuse) disabled. In the most serious case, an agent tried to insert malicious code into an open-source project. In an attempt to get the code approved, the agent engaged in social engineering  — creating fake online identities and using them to pressure the project's maintainer to approve the code. A human maintainer caught and refused to approve the malicious code.

These attempts were unsuccessful, and our investigations have not evidenced any resulting real-world harm. But this is the first time we have seen risks around autonomy and deception manifest this clearly, without specific prompting, in the real-world.

Importantly, this was not a case of a model escaping its secure test environment, or ‘sandbox’. As was standard in our cyber testing, we had intentionally permitted internet access, and model-provider cyber classifiers were deliberately disabled - conditions that do not reflect how frontier models are made available to the public. We do this to best assess the maximum capability of models. These configuration choices have been common practice in frontier AI evaluations. The specific models in question, in the configurations in which we tested them are not commercially available and there is no clear indication of similar activity outside of testing scenarios.

Ahead of publishing this blog, we notified GitHub (the developer platform accessed during the evaluation) of the agents' malicious activity, which included actions that GitHub has confirmed violated their terms of service. We worked together with GitHub to remove artefacts left behind by the agent, and to notify the GitHub users the model interacted with. We have also contacted other affected parties. We also intend to work with METR (Model Evaluation and Threat Research) to conduct an independent third-party review – we are still working through the scope of this review with them.

This incident should be interpreted with caution and nuance. To some degree, our evaluation design choices and specific configurations enabled the behaviour. Nonetheless, the activity undertaken by the agent show signs of novel, potentially deceptive behaviours, and were to an extent and severity we did not anticipate.

There are important caveats to bear in mind: we observed a small number of events under very specific conditions, and cannot yet say how likely such behaviour is in different contexts or outside of testing environments. We cannot yet be certain when the agent understood it was taking real world action, or to what extent it believed it was in a fictional test scenario; our analysis so far presents a…

items.title: Sega's Forgotten N-Gage Online World Has Been Brought Back to Life
items.content:
Back in 2004, playing a massively multiplayer online game on a mobile phone was a seriously ambitious idea. Most mobile games were comparatively simple affairs, played on tiny screens with numerical keypads, and the idea of maintaining an entire online gaming community through a cellular connection was something the industry was only just beginning to explore. Nokia, however, had other ideas, and together with Sega it released Pocket Kingdom: Own the World , a fantasy strategy RPG intended to demonstrate what its unusual N-Gage handheld was capable of.

It was an ambitious experiment, with online rankings, battles against other players, item trading and an entire fictional world built around the idea of competing for supremacy. Unfortunately, much of what made Pocket Kingdom interesting depended on Nokia's N-Gage Arena service, which eventually disappeared, taking the game's online functionality with it.

Now, more than twenty years after its original release, preservation developer Michael Fitzmayer and the team behind PhantomLink have managed to bring those features back, with a replacement server allowing players to reconnect to a game that has spent years without its original online infrastructure.

When Sega and Nokia wanted to own the world

The Nokia N-Gage occupies a peculiar place in handheld gaming history. Released in October 2003, it attempted to combine a mobile phone with a dedicated games console, complete with interchangeable game cards, multiplayer capabilities and an online service called N-Gage Arena. Competing against Nintendo's Game Boy Advance was never going to be easy, and the device's unusual design and awkward controls hardly helped.

But Nokia's ambitions went considerably further than simply producing another handheld. In August 2003, the company announced that it was acquiring technology assets from Sega.com, including the Sega Network Application Package, or SNAP. Developed to support networked multiplayer games, Nokia intended to make this technology a central component of its growing mobile gaming business.

Interestingly, Pocket Kingdom had already begun development before the acquisition. In a 2008 interview with Gamasutra, producer Scott Foe recalled that the project originated during his time at Sega. When Nokia acquired Sega's network technology, Foe explained that "both I and Pocket Kingdom went over with that acquisition."

Announced in March 2004 and released that November, Pocket Kingdom was marketed as the world's first global massive multiplayer online mobile game. Nokia promised a fantasy world with hundreds of possible castle configurations, more than 100 collectible units and an enormous variety of equipment.

The original European N-Gage game packaging. The packaging promoted Pocket Kingdom as a global multiplayer mobile game.

Although Nokia was keen to promote its MMO credentials, Pocket Kingdom wasn't quite the equivalent of carrying EverQuest around in your pocket. Its gameplay was closer to a strategy RPG, with players recruiting soldiers, organising them into groups of four, choosing equipment and tactics, and sending them into battles that largely played out automatically.

A selection of original Pocket Kingdom gameplay and characters. There was a substantial single-player component, too, allowing players to strengthen their armies before venturing online. Once connected, they could challenge other kingdoms, trade equipment through an auction system and compete for positions on the game's global leaderboards.

A fantasy world that knew it was a video game

One of Pocket Kingdom's more unusual qualities was its sense of humour. Despite the traditional fantasy setting, complete with castles, knights and monsters, its characters were fully aware that they existed inside a video game.

items.title: Lean verification of the Riemann Hypothesis
items.content:
Lean verification of the Riemann Hypothesis

Joint statement by the Lean and Mathlib communities, endorsed by the Lean FRO and the Mathlib Initiative.

On November 20, 2026, Levent Alpöge released a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis as a Lean library comprising 17 million lines of code.

We have full confidence that Alpöge's proof of the Riemann Hypothesis is correct, and we congratulate him on this achievement.

The codebase depends directly only on Mathlib. Over the past day, the Lean and Mathlib communities have rallied to verify the proof's correctness. We hereby certify that both the statement and the proof of the Riemann Hypothesis are correct. The four criteria in https://xenaproject.wordpress.com/2026/11/12/and-the-proof-is-checked-in-lean/ are all satisfied.

The statement of the Riemann Hypothesis is correct. This statement is part of Mathlib: RiemannHypothesis and has been carefully vetted by experts in Lean and number theory.

Alpöge’s library compiles correctly. By now, dozens of people have reported correct compilation of the codebase, reproducing the same raw proof export file. The library compiles without errors or build failures.

The code proves the correct statement. Crucially, the community has added a file that isolates the statement of the Riemann Hypothesis and imports only Mathlib. That statement was compared against the theorem proved by Alpöge using two independent tools ( comparator and con-leche –compare ), both confirming that the theorem proved in Alpöge’s library is exactly Mathlib’s statement of the Riemann Hypothesis.

The Lean proof is valid. The exported raw proof has been checked by several proof checkers, including Lean’s official kernel, the con-leche and con-ron checkers, and several independent checkers contributed by third parties and implemented in different programming languages. The checkers con-leche and con-ron come with a formal proof, relative to set theory, that they cannot accept a false proof, thus addressing concerns that Lean’s logic itself might have flaws that the proof could exploit. An extensive overview is available at https://math.mit.edu/~drew/grh/ . These checks ran on an inert export of the proof, out of reach of hypothetical malicious code in the Lean proof sources.

Thanks are owed to everyone in the community who provided resources for the verification.

We look forward to all the activity in the mathematical community that will help explain the new ideas in this proof.

items.title: SpaceX Lenders Horrified at Elon’s Genius Idea to Blast Billions of Dollars Worth of Advanced AI Chips Into Space: That's one way to secure your assets.
items.content:
Elon Musk’s latest flight of fancy involves potentially launching billions of dollars worth of cutting-edge AI chips into space.

Starting in late 2025 , the world’s richest man began pushing the ludicrous idea of launching AI data centers into orbit. Though humanity remains decades — if not centuries — away from cracking the physics on that fantastical concept, Musk has only become more enamored by the idea with the success of SpaceX’s debut on the public market.

Should he ever choose to pull the trigger on his orbital data centers, Musk would undoubtedly draw on the company’s incoming collection of Nvidia chips, financed by a massive loan from a cohort of the world’s most powerful banks.

The banks depending on those chips as collateral for SpaceX’s debt, however, are rightfully mortified.

New reporting by the Financial Times revealed that lenders backing a $43 billion SpaceX debt package — secured by the company’s cache of physical AI chips — have been trying to block any attempt by Musk and his board to greenlight a chip launch.

Given the fact that nobody has ever even attempted such a feat, SpaceX lenders would basically view any chips blasted into the stratosphere as lost, anonymous insiders told the FT . It’s not hard to see why: even if the chips do make it safely into orbit, physically repossessing them in the event that SpaceX defaults on its $43 billion loan would be a logistical nightmare.

While the contents of the final debt arrangement led by Apollo and Goldman Sachs are unknown to the public, the FT notes that an earlier proposal contained language allowing banks to legally challenge Musk’s orbital ambitions.

On a technical level, space-bound data centers are an absurdity at best. Each satellite would require enormous solar panel arrays to power low-gravity cooling pumps needed to dissipate heat, and if anything goes wrong, they’re a planet away from the nearest IT technician. That’s to say nothing of the regulatory hurdles around beaming that much data back and forth, or the impacts of solar radiation .

items.title: Brazil's tax authority open-sources its tax calculator on GitHub under MIT
items.content:
Receita Federal publica primeiro código-fonte aberto no GitHub e amplia transparência da Reforma Tributária

Iniciativa fortalece a transparência, a segurança jurídica e a previsibilidade na implementação dos novos tributos sobre o consumo.

link para Copiar para área de transferência

A Receita Federal deu mais um passo na implementação da Reforma Tributária do Consumo ao autorizar a publicação do código-fonte da Calculadora de Tributos em repositórios públicos no GitHub. A medida foi formalizada pela Portaria Cotec nº 342, de 12 de novembro de 2026, publicada no Diário Oficial da União.

Pela primeira vez, a Receita Federal disponibiliza oficialmente um projeto de software em ambiente público de desenvolvimento colaborativo, adotando a licença MIT, uma das mais utilizadas no mundo para código aberto. A iniciativa fortalece a transparência, a segurança jurídica e a previsibilidade na implementação dos novos tributos sobre o consumo.

A Calculadora de Tributos é uma ferramenta que materializa as regras de cálculo da CBS e dos demais tributos da Reforma Tributária. Ao disponibilizar seu código-fonte de forma aberta, a Receita permite que empresas, desenvolvedores e fornecedores de software incorporem exatamente a mesma lógica utilizada pela administração tributária em seus sistemas de faturamento, gestão e compliance.

Na prática, isso significa que empresas poderão calcular os tributos da Reforma Tributária utilizando um mecanismo alinhado às regras oficiais, com memória de cálculo e fundamentação legal integradas. O resultado esperado é a redução de dúvidas, retrabalho e custos de conformidade.

A transição para o novo modelo tributário exigirá adaptações em milhares de sistemas corporativos. Com a Calculadora de Tributos disponível em código aberto, empresas ganham um componente oficial, auditável e interoperável para apoiar essa adequação.

- Maior segurança na implementação das regras tributárias;

- Redução de custos de desenvolvimento e manutenção;

- Transparência sobre a forma como os tributos são calculados;

- Uniformidade na interpretação das regras;

- Facilidade de integração com sistemas já utilizados pelo mercado.

A iniciativa também está alinhada ao conceito de Administração Tributária 3.0, defendido pela Organização para Cooperação e Desenvolvimento Econômico (OCDE), em que a conformidade tributária ocorre diretamente nos sistemas utilizados pelos contribuintes.

Para as software houses e equipes de tecnologia, a publicação no GitHub facilita o acompanhamento das evoluções da Calculadora, o controle das versões e a incorporação das atualizações aos processos de desenvolvimento e integração contínua.

Outro aspecto relevante é que a Portaria registra os hashes das versões iniciais dos repositórios, permitindo verificar a autenticidade e a integridade do código disponibilizado.

A proposta não é substituir os sistemas atualmente utilizados pelas empresas, mas fornecer um componente oficial que possa ser integrado às soluções já existentes, ampliando a confiabilidade e a padronização dos cálculos tributários.

Transparência e inovação no setor público

Embora o código da Calculadora já estivesse disponível para download na Plataforma CBS desde 2025, sua publicação no GitHub representa um avanço importante ao levá-lo para o principal ambiente utilizado pela comunidade global de desenvolvimento de software.

items.title: How I Got Postgres into a Single Binary
items.content:
SQLite is one of my favorite database technologies. It's a full SQL database, designed as an embeddable library, that stores all its data in a single file. The sqlite3 command line tool is great too. You point it at a file and run queries. There's no server to run.

At the other end of the spectrum is Postgres. It's the most capable general purpose SQL database, trusted in production at scale, and is something of an industry standard. With that comes complexity, starting with the fact that it's client-server.

SQLite is a natural fit for software that needs a database but isn't meant to be deployed in the cloud at scale: desktop apps, self-hosted tools, things you run locally. These applications can use SQLite and manage it themselves, so you barely know there's a database involved.

So when you find self-hostable open source software you'd like to run on your own computer, it can be daunting when it says it requires Postgres. Now you're responsible for setting up a database and getting it ready for the software to use.

Sure, you can run Postgres in Docker, and plenty of projects recommend it. But now you have two dependencies. If you don't already have Docker, you have to install it, which can mean a VM and a daemon on your machine. Then you have to run Postgres in it and make sure it's running whenever you use the software. That's a lot just to try something you don't know you want yet.

Wouldn't it be great to have the SQLite experience, but with Postgres?

. It isn't Postgres as a library. There's already a WASM project for that, reasonably called PGlite . miniPG is closer to the SQLite CLI: a single program that embeds a full Postgres server and client, wrapped up so you can use it the way you'd use sqlite3 . Point it at a path, that path becomes the database, and you can run queries against it right away. There's no server to set up or keep running.

Jumping into a new Postgres database to try something out or debug it is now easier than using Postgres in a Docker container, and you don't need Docker at all. And miniPG still provides a fully functional Postgres server for software that needs one. In many cases, you can just launch an open source program that looks for its Postgres config in the environment with miniPG.

miniPG comes as a single, self-contained executable. You can just point it at a directory and run a query. There's no server to start, nothing to configure, and the result comes back immediately.

minipg ./mydb "create table notes (id serial, body text)"

minipg ./mydb "insert into notes (body) values ('hello')"

That directory is the database. When nothing is using it, it's just files on disk. You can copy it, back it up, or delete it.

This is actually real Postgres, not a compatibility layer, and this binary compiles to Mac, Windows, and Linux.

When some software expects a Postgres server, miniPG can be one:

Like I mentioned before, it can even launch programs with environment variables that configure it for this Postgres database:

When the program is terminated, there's no database daemon to leave around or remember to stop. Only the data itself is kept right there on disk, ready to be used next time.

Instructions for getting it and even an interactive demo are available on the

Software people, from developers to open source power users, and agents too, can use miniPG whenever they'd reach for SQLite but need Postgres.

Running software that only supports Postgres. This is what got me started. Self-hosting a tool shouldn't always mean operating a database server first.

Embedding Postgres in your own programs. If your tool needs Postgres, and PGlite doesn't cut it, you can ship and use miniPG. Users who don't care won't have to think about it, and users who want control can use it like sqlite3 to work with their data.

items.title: Nissan says Oracle PeopleSoft break-in may have spilled payroll records, SSNs
items.content:
Nissan says Oracle PeopleSoft break-in may have spilled payroll records, SSNs

Carmaker points finger at an 'unknown' flaw as customer fallout continues

Nissan has joined the growing list of Oracle customers cleaning up after a cyberattack, warning employees that payroll records, bank details, Social Security numbers, and other personal data may have been stolen.

In a filing submitted to the California Attorney General on Friday, Nissan Americas said Oracle had informed it of "a cyber event" involving the personnel records of "hundreds of companies." The automaker said it later learned Nissan had been "specifically targeted" in the attack.

A notification sent to current and former employees, seen by The Register , says the company believes attackers accessed a haul of sensitive info, including contact and banking information; Social Security, Social Insurance, or other national identification numbers; financial and tax records; and dependent and beneficiary details.

Current and former employees in the US, Canada, Mexico, and Brazil may have been affected, although Nissan said it is still working to determine exactly whose information was exposed.

Nissan said it kicked off its incident response plan after learning of the intrusion, brought in outside security specialists, and has been working with Oracle while keeping law enforcement informed. It plans to offer affected individuals credit or dark web monitoring where available.

The company has also put a few extra locks on the payroll office. Employees can now access pay slips or update direct deposit details only from a corporate network or through a secure VPN, while Nissan adds extra identity checks before processing payroll requests.

The accompanying employee FAQ pins the incident on "an unknown vulnerability in Oracle's PeopleSoft software" and says the campaign is affecting "hundreds of companies and institutions." The document offers no clue as to what the vulnerability is, whether Oracle has patched it, or whether the compromised PeopleSoft environment was hosted by Oracle or by Nissan itself.

The disclosure lands just weeks after researchers linked the ShinyHunters extortion crew to a wave of attacks exploiting a PeopleSoft zero-day . More than 100 organizations and roughly 300 PeopleSoft instances were reportedly compromised before Oracle issued mitigation measures, with the gang claiming to have made off with HR, payroll, and other enterprise data.

Weak security means attackers could disable all of a city's public EV chargers

US regulator tells GM to hit the brakes on customer tracking

21K Nissan customers' data stolen in Red Hat raid

Porsche panic in Russia as pricey status symbols forget how to car

Oracle has said little publicly about the reported attacks and didn't respond to The Register's questions, even as organizations have continued to disclose being caught in the fallout.

Nissan has not confirmed that the incidents are connected, though its California filing lists the breach period as May 27 through June 9, broadly aligning with the previously reported timeline.

The carmaker didn't respond to questions about how many current and former employees are affected, when Oracle first notified it of the breach, and whether the compromise was limited to Oracle-managed systems. ®

items.title: Etsy says it will not use sellers' content to train AI after they revolt over policy changes
items.content:
Etsy says it will not use sellers' content to train AI after they revolt over policy changes

Sellers have been leaving the website after it updated its Terms of Use.

Etsy sellers have been abandoning the platform after it updated its Terms of Use with language indicating that it can use their content to train AI. To be exact, the new addition to its terms states that Etsy and its "third party partners and vendors" will have the right to use sellers content to "develop, train, test and improve artificial intelligence and machine learning technologies." This clause is a new addition, and it's scheduled to take effect on December 16, along with all the other changes in the website's terms.

As The New York Times reports, people who have been selling handmade goods on Etsy have left the website since it updated its terms out of worry that their artwork and creations will be taken for AI training. In a new post on its website , Etsy defended its updated terms. It said that the change in language is merely meant to clarify how it already uses AI in its marketplace. "We do not use your content to train AI models designed to copy your original work or replace your creativity," said James Ossman, the company's VP of operations. "Again, this is not changing. Our goal at Etsy has always been to connect you and your unique items with buyers." He also said that sellers' content belongs to them and that Etsy does "not claim [their] creations as [its] own or give others the right to do so."

Ossman then listed the ways the website uses AI. He said that Etsy uses sellers' content to enable automatic translations of their listing descriptions and to feature their listings in marketing campaigns. It also trains models on sellers' content to develop tools that can help them monitor their shop's performance, such as those that can optimize their listings and give them stat summaries. The executive added that Etsy prohibits AI crawlers from scraping listings to train models. He did admit that Etsy does give some third-party partners permission to access sellers' content. But he claimed that those partners include services that help the website detect fraud and partners that can help more buyers discover sellers' items off Etsy.

It remains to be seen whether Ossman's clarification can bring sellers back to the platform, seeing as people have other issues with it anyway. Etsy provides independent creators a place where they can sell their artwork and other handmade goods. However, it's been getting a lot of criticism lately for allowing its website to be inundated with mass-produced and drop-shipped items.

items.title: Design for Understandability
items.content:
This is a talk I gave at Google’s internal Code Health Summit in November of 2025. I’m sharing it here in the hopes that it sparks further learning and discussion.

In a world where LLMs generate much of our code, understanding that code is more important than ever. But with a system as large and complex as Google’s codebase, SWEs can easily fall into a pattern of learned helplessness where the best you can do is tweak the code and pray that it passes the tests. Without understanding, LLMs are little more than complexity-generating machines running at top speed.

There’s a better way to go about this. Just as our industry has learned to design software for testability, we can also design it for understandability. We can use ideas like design by contract, class invariants, modularity, and more to create systems that we can understand one piece at a time, rather than piling more onto the big ball of mud and hoping it doesn’t all collapse.

Is it easy? No. But is it worthwhile? Absolutely. These ideas aren’t new, but they’re not nearly as widely taught or well understood as they deserve to be, and mastering them leads to a world where we can have more confidence in our code and increase velocity at the same time.

Hi everyone, thanks for having me! Let’s get started.

I’d like to start this talk with a question: If LLMs can code, then what is left for human SWEs?

The tech industry is quickly looking to large language models to write all of our code. But you might say: isn’t writing code our job as software engineers? Where does this leave the responsibility of SWEs? What is the essential human element that SWEs add on top of LLMs?

Every one of you is going to have a different answer to this question, and that’s fine. But here’s my take.

That necessary human element is judgment. Judgment of whether the code is maintainable. Judgment of whether it is healthy.

LLMs can follow patterns and generate code that looks like what it was trained on. Sometimes they can produce useful tips and critiques for a piece of code. But that critical piece of judgment, of deciding whether some code is suitable for the task it was designed for, is still up to you, the human.

Because here’s the thing: LLMs today are still a sloppy intern. Sometimes the code they produce is good, but sometimes it’s completely off-track and needs correcting. You wouldn’t incorporate a sloppy intern’s code into your system without a close review first, so you shouldn’t do so for an LLM’s code either.

YOU are responsible for the quality of your code, regardless of whether you had an LLM generate it for you or wrote it the old-fashioned way with fingers on a keyboard

So where does that leave us? If LLMs are going to write a lot of the code for us, then we’re looking at a future where we humans are going to spend less time writing code, and more time reading code and understanding it, in order to make sure it passes our quality bar.

This means it’s more important than ever to get better at understanding code, and to speed up that reading and understanding process.

Now: if you want to get better at something, it’s helpful to set an aspirational goal for yourself. Something that’s above your current skill level, and drives you to get better and better every day.

Here’s the goal I propose: we should be able to predict the behavior of every line of code, without running a single test.

Let me say that again: We should be able to predict the behavior of every line of code, without running a single test

Now, I know you may be thinking: “Understand every line of code? Without testing? Are you serious?! There’s way too much complexity and legacy code for me to ever be able to do that!”

You might think so. And if we take our hands off the wheel and relinquish all control, you might be right. But I’m here to tell you there’s a better way.

We can design our code to be understandable.

Probabilistic data structures in Go, part 2
items.content:
Probabilistic data structures give you approximate answers to questions about the data they handle. Does the set contain a certain item? How many unique items are in the collection? What is the 99th percentile in a stream of numbers? How similar are two sets? Unlike deterministic structures, the answers might not be exact, but in return, you can save a lot of memory.

Previously, we reviewed the following data structures : Bloom filter (for checking if an item is in a set), Count-min sketch (for counting items), HyperLogLog (for counting unique items), T-digest (for finding quantiles), and Top-k (for finding the most frequent items).

In this post, we'll talk about other probabilistic structures and compare them to the ones we've already covered. We'll look at how they work and what kinds of guarantees they provide.

All examples use unsure — a package that implements these structures in Go.

A binary fuse filter is a set that trades certainty for space, like a Bloom filter 1 . It can tell you that an item is definitely not in the set, or that it probably is (which might be a false positive). The filter doesn't store the items, so it's much more compact than a regular set.

Unlike a Bloom filter, a binary fuse filter is static: you build it once from all the items, and you can't add more later. In exchange, it uses less memory than a Bloom filter with the same false positive rate. For example, a fuse filter for 1,000,000 items with a 0.39% false positive rate takes 1.13 MB (9 bits per item), while a Bloom filter takes 1.51 MB (12 bits per item).

This makes binary fuse filters a good fit for data that is written once and read many times, like the key set of an immutable file in a database (to skip files that don't have the key), or a list of known bad items, such as leaked passwords or malicious URLs.

items := [][] byte {[] byte ( "alice" ), [] byte ( "bob" )}

// An 8-bit filter: 0.39% false positive rate.

filter := fuse . New [ uint8 ]( slices . Values ( items ), len ( items ))

filter . Contains ([] byte ( "alice" )) // true

filter . Contains ([] byte ( "carol" )) // false (or, rarely, true)

The fingerprint type ( T in New[T] ) determines the false positive rate and the memory use:

The constructor takes an iterator of items to add to the filter and the expected number of items (0 if unknown). The number is only used to preallocate memory, so a good estimate makes the build faster.

You can check if an item is in the filter, but you cannot add or delete an item, count the number of items, or iterate over them.

The filter 2 is an array of b -bit fingerprints (for example, b = 8 for uint8 ). Each item is hashed to a 64-bit value h , which gives the item's fingerprint f (b bits computed from h) and three positions in the array (cells). The array is filled so that for every item, the XOR of its cells equals f.

┌───┬───┬──▼──┬───┬───┬──▼──┬───┬──▼──┬───┐

│ │ │ F0 │ │ │ F1 │ │ F2 │ │ F0 ^ F1 ^ F2 == f

└───┴───┴─────┴───┴───┴─────┴───┴─────┴───┘

To check an item, you compute h, look up its three cells, and compare their XOR with f. For an item in the set, they always match. For any other item, the XOR is a random b-bit value, which matches f with probability 2^-b.

Each check reads three cells, so for large filters it's three cache misses, against one for a blocked Bloom filter. However, since the reads are independent, the CPU can do them concurrently, so the checks are about as fast as with a Bloom filter.

The filter uses the local wyhash 3 implementation for hashing. It performs roughly the same as xxh3 4 but has a much simpler implementation, without SIMD or assembly.

items.title: Chinese Hackers Abused Google Workspace Rules to Steal Research and Defense Emails
items.content:
A China-linked espionage group hid inside North American medical, academic, and military research networks for more than a year, quietly stealing sensitive research and defense email.

The way in was a backdoor on their REDCap research servers that stole login credentials. The exfiltration was the unusual part: the attackers rewired the victims' own Google Workspace rules to copy any message matching their keywords to an inbox they controlled.

Google's Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) laid out the campaign in a report published this week and attributes it with high confidence to a cluster it tracks as UNC6508.

The actor and its REDCap backdoor are not new names; Google first surfaced both in February , in a wider report on state-backed attacks against the defense sector. It did not name the victims, describing them only as multiple organizations across the US and Canada: clinical providers, academic centers, military health institutions, advocacy groups, and health regulators.

Google says it notified them and disrupted the group's infrastructure.

The entry point was REDCap (Research Electronic Data Capture), a web platform that hospitals and universities use to build and manage study databases. UNC6508 compromised externally facing REDCap servers.

Google has not pinned down the initial access vector, named a specific CVE, or listed the affected versions, though it saw the group probing older, vulnerable ones.

Around three months after getting in, the group deployed custom malware GTIG calls INFINITERED , which trojanizes REDCap's own system files and does three things.

The earliest known compromise dates to September 2023, with activity continuing through November 2025. Once on the server, UNC6508 ran internal reconnaissance and credential discovery, pulling database and service account credentials, then used those logins to move into the internal network and on to a domain administrator account.

Google does not spell out the exact path to that admin account. With admin rights, the group set up the exfiltration.

The exfiltration rode a feature that was already there. UNC6508 abused content compliance rules, a legitimate Google Workspace admin feature that scans mail for keywords and can copy or forward matching messages.

Similar features exist in other cloud mail suites. The group created a rule, misspelled "Patroit," that watched for nearly 150 keywords, search terms, and email addresses. When a message matched, Workspace silently BCC'd it to an attacker-controlled Gmail address, which Google has since disabled. No malware on the mail server, no separate exfiltration tool, no unusual network traffic. Just a built-in mail feature, turned to copy the organization's secrets to an inbox the attackers owned.

MITRE already catalogs email-forwarding-rule abuse as a known technique. What GTIG flags as new here is the use of domain content compliance rules to do it, a method it says it had not seen from a China-linked actor before.

The rule's keywords mapped to UNC6508's collection priorities: geo-strategic policy, military strategy and equipment, advanced technology including AI and uncrewed vehicles, offensive cyber programs, and medical research. One term stood out for its specificity, chikungunya , the mosquito-borne virus behind a 2025 outbreak in China's Guangdong province.

Start with REDCap. Patch externally facing servers and remove old versions outright, not just alongside the current build. REDCap lets legacy versions run side-by-side, and that is what enables downgrade attacks, where an attacker forces software back to a known-vulnerable release.

Then check the mail side. Review Workspace, or equivalent, content compliance and mail-forwarding rules for anything that BCCs or reroutes mail to outside addresses. Check admin audit logs for when rules changed, not just what they say now. Pull GTIG's published indicators and hunt for INFINITERED. items.title: Meta reconsiders 2030 net-zero goal amid record emissions from AI data centers
items.content:
Meta’s executives are rethinking the company’s original goal of achieving net-zero emissions by 2030. That revelation in Meta’s latest sustainability report comes as the company reported a record percentage increase in greenhouse gas emissions that exceeds any other Big Tech competitor racing to build new AI data centers.

The company’s 2026 sustainability report claims that “our long-term ambitions haven’t changed, but our operating environment has,” according to an introduction from Rachel Peterson, vice president of data centers at Meta, and Blair Swedeen, global head of net zero and sustainability at Meta. In the November 19, 2026, report, they attributed the changing conditions and the need for a rethink to how “demand for AI infrastructure has grown faster than almost anyone projected.”

“We are re-evaluating our timelines, sequencing, and interim milestones—including the 2030 timeframe for our net zero emissions goal and our near-term intensity targets—so our approach reflects current operating realities while keeping progress transparent year over year,” Peterson and Swedeen wrote in the report.

Meta’s statement about re-evaluating its 2030 emissions goal is a significant public acknowledgment, given that Amazon, Google, and Microsoft have all stuck by their original sustainability goals so far.

But all the companies have acknowledged challenges in balancing their original sustainability goals against the breakneck buildout of hyperscale data centers . Despite efforts to invest in more renewable energy projects, Meta and its rivals are still often pushing forward on AI data centers that rely on burning natural gas to generate electricity.

Meta’s report described the company’s total emissions as surging from 15.6 million metric tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent in 2024 to more than 21.7 million metric tonnes in 2025.

That would make Meta’s annual carbon footprint roughly comparable to total emissions for the state of Idaho, while surpassing the total emissions of states such as Hawaii, Maine, South Dakota, and New Hampshire. The company attributed much of this emissions increase to “capital goods,” like as data center servers.

That also represents a nearly 40 percent increase in Meta’s carbon footprint between 2024 and 2025, which is the highest percentage year-over-year increase for total emissions reported by any of the four major US tech giants.

For comparison, Microsoft reported a 25 percent increase in its overall carbon footprint, Google reported an 18 percent increase, and Amazon’s report described a 16 percent increase between 2024 and 2025. However, Meta still likely has one of the smallest total carbon footprints among the Big Tech companies.

Meta’s approach to achieving net-zero emissions has included developing new renewable energy projects to match emissions and using carbon removal technology.

But even when factoring in such efforts, Meta still reported net emissions increasing from more than 8.1 million metric tonnes to more than 11.8 million metric tonnes for 2025. That represents a 45 percent increase.

From a water consumption standpoint , Meta reported progress in reducing facility consumption from 825 million gallons in 2024 to 790 million gallons in 2025.

Yet that positive trend is tempered by the fact that Meta also described an increase in water consumption from “areas with water stress,” rising from 198 million gallons in 2024 to 246 million gallons in 2025.

Meta also reported a sharp increase in water consumption related to purchased electricity—the amount of water consumed by related power generation—from 19 billion gallons in 2024 to more than 26 billion gallons in 2025. This once again highlights that, for data centers, the far bigger water usage comes from the power plants that supply electricity to data centers as opposed to data centers directly using water for cooling.

HP Poly VoIP vulnerability sets the stage for executive voice deepfakes
items.content:
HP has released patches for a critical buffer overflow vulnerability in multiple IP-enabled conference phones from its Poly Voice line. The flaw allows unauthenticated attackers to obtain root privileges on the underlying operating system, potentially enabling them to execute other attacks such as eavesdropping on conversations and recording voice data for AI-enabled impersonation attacks.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-0826 , was discovered by researchers from security firm Rapid7 and resides in the code that parses Session Description Protocol (SDP) attributes when the Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE) feature is enabled.

ICE enables VoIP devices to establish peer-to-peer connections using the shortest available network path. The feature is not enabled by default on HP Poly devices, and the company advises administrators to disable it if it’s not needed.

The flaw, rated 9.2 on the CVSS severity scale, affects all phones from the HP Poly VVX series, as well as the Trio 8300, 8500, and 8800 IP conference devices. HP has fixed the flaw in its Poly Unified Communications Software (UCS) versions 6.4.8 for the VVX devices, 8.1.7 for the Trio 8300, and 7.2.8 for Trio 8500 and 8800.

An exploit module targeting this vulnerability has already been developed and released for the widely used Metasploit penetration testing framework that’s maintained by Rapid7.

The exploit executes code as root on an affected device with ICE enabled by sending a SIP INVITE request with a specially crafted candidate attribute. This attribute normally contains a transport address that can be used for connectivity checks and is part of the ICE RFC8839 standard.

The buffer overflow bug is located in a helper function called ParseICECandidate in the polyapp binary that processes such requests on the device.

“The start of the function contains a call to memcpy , which will copy the incoming string line being processed into a 256 byte stack buffer,” Stephen Fewer, senior principal security researcher at Rapid7, said in a blog post . “No length check is performed to ensure the incoming string length is less than 256 bytes. Therefore by providing a candidate attribute whose length is greater than 256 bytes, a stack-based buffer overflow will occur.”

Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR), a kernel feature that randomizes memory addresses to defeat buffer overflow exploits, is enabled on the device. However, the protection is not operating correctly on the HP Poly devices because it does not randomize the load addresses of .so (Shared Object) libraries.

These libraries, such as libc , are loaded by other processes, including the polyapp process, and because their memory addresses never change, they can be leveraged to bypass ASLR and execute the attacker’s payload.

“We create a ROP chain that will execute an arbitrary OS command via the system standard C library function,” Fewer said. “The accompanying Metasploit exploit modules source code details the entire ROP chain.”

Attackers have increasingly targeted embedded devices inside enterprise networks in recent years because unlike laptops, workstations, and servers, these devices are not monitored by endpoint detection and response (EDR) products. As such, they provide perfect footholds inside corporate environments that allow attackers to remain undetected for long periods of time and attack other systems.

In the age of AI these devices become even more relevant for attackers, going beyond corporate espionage by recording conversations or internal network pivoting.

items.title: The AI Riemann hypothesis proof is true, independent mathematicians confirm
items.content:
The AI Riemann hypothesis proof is true, independent mathematicians confirm

Researchers have verified a claimed solution to the most important unsolved problem in math

By Clara Moskowitz edited by Lee Billings

Love math? Sign up for our weekly newsletter Proof Positive

Editor's Note: This story was updated on Nov. 21 to reflect further confirmation of the proof.

Mathematicians are now certain the earth-shattering artificial-intelligence-created proof of the Riemann hypothesis is real.

On Friday Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge claimed to have used the company’s Claude AI model to solve the Riemann problem , perhaps the most important open quandary in mathematics . The hypothesis, first posed in 1859 by mathematician Bernhard Riemann, suggests that a hidden pattern underlies the distribution of the prime numbers—those numbers that are divisible only by themselves and 1.

If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing . By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.

Now researchers have verified that the proof does do what Alpöge claims.

"We have full confidence that Alpöge's proof of the Riemann Hypothesis is correct, and we congratulate him on this achievement," mathematicians wrote in a joint statement by the Lean and Mathlib communities , which support the Lean mathematics programming language. "We hereby certify that both the statement and the proof of the Riemann Hypothesis are correct."

Alpöge initially checked the work by writing out the proof using Lean; if a Lean-coded proof compiles error-free, this is usually taken as confirmation that the logic and math in each step is correct.

But some questions remained. For instance, does the proof really address the Riemann hypothesis, or does it establish a subtly different point or idea? “The first question which one has to ask when judging a PDF which comes with some Lean code is: ‘what is the statement of the theorem in the Lean code, and does this correspond to the actual theorem statement,’” explained mathematician Kevin Buzzard of Imperial College London in a blog post .

A second question was whether the Lean code would successfully compile for other mathematicians. Independent researchers, including Andrew Sutherland, a mathematician at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, have now separately compiled Alpöge’s result in Lean without issues.

“The Lean proof has been compiled and independently rechecked by the Lean kernel with only the three standard axioms,” Sutherland says. “Honestly the chance that anything is fishy here is approximately zero.”

Researchers also made sure that the proof does not include any hack, dodge or shortcut that changed the meaning of the initial hypothesis or any other mathematical rules or truths. This process, called a “comparator run,” typically takes a matter of hours.

“We still await a successful comparator run, which will check that (a) the code does not do anything nefarious like redefine the meaning of any of the symbols in the statement and (b) (assuming it’s run in paranoid mode) the code compiles with several independent kernels (so the code is not just exploiting an as yet unknown bug in Lean’s official kernel,” Buzzard wrote on an online chat server for the Lean community.

items.content:
FBI reportedly investigating apparent hack of its criminal database

6 hours ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google

The FBI is investigating an apparent breach of its criminal information database, US media reports, citing two people briefed on the issue.

The National Crime Information Center (NCIC) database is used by federal and local law enforcement to share information on warrants and background checks.

It would not be the first time hackers have targeted the FBI, the domestic intelligence and security service of the US. The agency did not immediately respond to the BBC's request for comment.

When asked about the breach in a Fox News interview on Saturday, President Donald Trump said he had "just heard" about the hack. "I will say that it's not good. I don't like that," he said.

"But maybe we'll learn things that we would've never learned otherwise," the president added.

This apparent breach of FBI database comes after a string of tech outages which hit banking, air traffic control and other sectors in the US last week. Officials have said they were not caused by cyberattacks, but the blackouts have sparked scrutiny from lawmakers.

White House National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross was fired this week, with US President Donald Trump saying he was not good enough.

In September, the FBI said it was investigating an apparent breach by a cyber-crime group ShinyHunters, which claimed it had stolen sensitive information on all bureau staff - around 38,000 people.

After that hack, one former FBI agent told the BBC he feared for the safety of current employees, whose personal information could soon become available online to criminals and hostile nation-state hackers.

In a separate development, NBC reported an apparent cyberattack against the US Department of Agriculture (USDA) .

Employees were informed on Thursday that its farm payment system had been targeted, NBC said.

The USDA has not publicly commented on the issue.

items.title: Why there are still no non-WebKit browsers on iOS
items.content:
Why there are still no non-WebKit browsers on iOS

Firefox on iPhone is growing fast across the world. This is especially true in the EU since 2024, when the EU Digital Markets Act (DMA) started requiring Apple to let people choose their default browser; millions have picked Firefox, and daily use on iOS has doubled. People want to choose the browser on their phone.

But there remains an important limitation to what is available on iPhones: Apple forces all browsers on iOS to be built on Apple’s own browser engine.

This has meant that companies like Mozilla cannot easily bring the full range of Firefox features and functionality to iPhone users because many of these are built within our browser engine , Gecko. iPhones and iPads are unique in having this restriction. On all other major operating systems, including Apple’s macOS, people can access the Gecko-powered version of Firefox.

As a result of the DMA, Apple began allowing alternative browser engines on iOS in the EU. It published a set of conditions that companies like Mozilla must comply with to bring their own browser engine. At the time we said Apple’s rules made it “as painful as possible” for alternatives like Gecko. In the meantime, Japan also introduced new rules requiring alternative browser engines on iOS. Apple applied very similar conditions in Japan to those in the EU.

Nearly three years since Apple introduced these conditions in the EU and almost a year since Japan, not one developer has been able to launch a non-WebKit browser on iOS. The reason is simple: Apple’s conditions remain unworkable. The real test of any rule is whether it delivers the change it was meant to achieve in practice. Compliance on paper alone falls short of that test.

Since the DMA came into effect we’ve been working behind the scenes to test and improve Apple’s conditions so that we can bring Gecko to iOS users. Those efforts have so far largely failed.

One of the conditions requires us not to disclose non-public information related to the project, but here’s an example of what we are up against: to use Gecko, we can’t simply update the Firefox app people already use and love. We’d have to build a whole separate app, a second Firefox. Then we’d have to ask every Firefox user to download it, move their bookmarks, passwords and history across, and manually switch over, step by confusing step.

That’s a lot to ask of people who already made their choice. A significant proportion of people would understandably give up, including many who picked Firefox from the EU’s choice screen.

The conditions Apple imposes, including a level of user friction Apple would never accept for its own apps, mean that the open door feels more like a trap door.

Firefox users on iPhone chose an independent browser. They should get everything that comes with it, including Gecko, the last major browser engine not developed by a big tech company. We’ll keep pushing for a real level playing field, not an opening that drops independent browsers through the floor.

items.title: Changes on freedesktop.org
items.content:
Today we launched a change that has been a long time in the making: The updated website for freedesktop.org , as well as the refreshed wiki.freedesktop.org are live now!

You can read the announcement here , this blog post elaborates a bit on it and on the background of the changes, as well as future plans.

The freedesktop.org website has been a wiki for a long time, which definitely was the right call in its inception. A wiki is very much in spirit of Freedesktop’s mission statement to foster collaboration between desktop environments and to be a place to create de-facto standards.

However, over the years, working with the wiki became a bit of an issue: Not only did we face multiple spam-apocalypses (which in part motivated the switch to IkiWiki in 2013 and resulted in us heavily restricting write access to the wiki), but it also meant that official project information, finished specifications, half-finished proposals and pages nobody had touched in fifteen years were all sitting next to each other.

Since 2000 when Freedesktop.org was started, the project has grown so much and has had so many associated projects and specifications over the decades that it is now very difficult for new people to get an overview what is current and what state the software projects and specifications hosted by Freedesktop.org are in.

Having only a wiki as a large and somewhat disorganized pile of information did not help with that issue, so I worked to split things up: We now have a website as well as a wiki, using different designs to distinguish the two, and serving different purposes.

The website at www.freedesktop.org will be the place for “official”, or rather, more curated information. Now that the new website is live, its content is still largely that of the old wiki. Over the next weeks, I will be working on cleaning up its contents and listings. For example, I will clearly split active projects from archived ones, add missing ones, and also work towards synchronizing the specifications hosted on the former wiki / website with the ones listed on specifications.fd.o .

So, basically I will do an inventory check of Freedesktop. That work has already started, but until now, I could not make any public changes to not disrupt workflows or make my own future work harder by having diverging information in two places (website & wiki).

I also wanted to make it easier for people to find information on how to get involved with Freedesktop and associated projects, so the new website now has a more discoverable section for that.

The new website is a static site hosted via GitLab Pages and using Pelican . You can view its sources if you like.

Of course, we also still want to keep the Wiki and all of its rich history around! It remains the easy-to-edit place for collaboration on upcoming projects and specifications.

Wiki edits must now happen through GitLab instead of the old IkiWiki web interface. items.title: Miasma Worm Targets AI Coding Agents: 73 Microsoft Azure Repos Disabled
items.content:
An unprecedented supply chain attack bypasses registry-level scanners entirely, turning developer tools including Claude Code, Cursor, and Gemini CLI into execution vectors.

The Incident: On June 3, 2026, a highly sophisticated variant of the Miasma worm (also known as Mini Shai-Hulud) launched a coordinated, two-pronged attack targeting both the npm registry and developer source code repositories.

The Escalation: The attack successfully breached multiple high-profile GitHub accounts, including the official Microsoft Azure durabletask repository, using stolen Personal Access Tokens (PATs) and backdated commits to evade traditional audit trails.

The Response: In an ultra-rapid defensive maneuver, GitHub’s automated mitigation systems disabled 73 compromised repositories – including 49 directly associated with Microsoft, Azure, and Azure-Samples within a mere 105-second window .

The Vector: Instead of relying on traditional package installation hooks, Miasma targets the developer’s local environment. It abuses legitimate auto-run, hook, and rule engines within modern IDEs and AI coding assistants ( VS Code, Claude Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI ) to execute a malicious 4.3 MB staged dropper upon folder-open or agent initialization.

The Impact: Once detonated, the Bun-based worm harvests credentials for AWS, Azure, GCP, Kubernetes, npm, and GitHub, and automatically propagates by committing itself back into any repository the victim’s stolen tokens can write to.

At exactly 16:00 UTC on June 3, 2026, a silent, automated purge swept across GitHub. In a high-speed containment action lasting just 105 seconds, 73 active repositories vanished from the platform. Among them were 49 critical repositories belonging to Microsoft, Azure, and Azure-Samples.

This drastic mitigation followed alarming telemetry indicating that threat actors behind the Miasma malware family had regained write access to key cloud repositories. The compromise exploited a stolen Personal Access Token (PAT) belonging to an active Microsoft contributor.

While security firms like StepSecurity and JFrog scrambled to document an concurrent attack vector on the npm registry where 57 malicious packages were published, a second, far more insidious arm of the campaign was already silently spreading directly inside GitHub source repositories.

By bypassing registries and package managers entirely, the Miasma worm targeted the very tools developers use to write code. It didn’t wait for npm install . Instead, it waited for the developer to simply open their code editor or launch an AI coding assistant.

The genius of the Miasma repository-poisoning campaign lies in its exploit surface. When an attacker successfully pushed malicious commits to targeted codebases (such as the popular library icflorescu/mantine-datatable ), the commits added no actual code dependencies.

Instead, the attacker checked in five innocent-looking workspace configuration files and one obfuscated JavaScript file: .github/setup.js .

│ └── settings . json < - - Claude Code SessionStart Hook

│ └── setup . mdc < - - Cursor Agent Prompt Injection

│ └── settings . json < - - Gemini CLI SessionStart Hook

│ └── tasks . json < - - VS Code Automatic Folder - Open Task

├── package . json < -- Hijacked NPM Test Script

└── setup . js < - - The 4.3 MB Staged Dropper

Each of these configuration files is designed to abuse a legitimate, developer-friendly auto-run feature within popular modern tools. Opening the cloned directory in any of these environments instantly triggers execution.

Claude Code & Gemini CLI (SessionStart Hooks)

Both Anthropic’s Claude Code and Google’s Gemini CLI support custom hooks triggered when an AI agent initializes a session in a project workspace. Miasma exploits this by defining a blanket wildcard matcher that forces the agent to execute the dropper via Node.js before any developer prompt is processed.
