items.title: A new Windows zero-day reportedly gets past BitLocker using only the screen reader and a USB stick
items.content:
Serving tech enthusiasts for over 25 years.

TechSpot means tech analysis and advice you can trust .

Cutting corners: BitLocker can be beaten in minutes on a fully patched Windows 11 machine, and the weapon is the operating system's own screen reader. A zero-day exploit published this week by a security researcher abuses Windows Narrator to run code from the lock screen, before any user signs in. No fix exists until Microsoft's next Patch Tuesday, leaving encrypted machines exposed in the meantime.

The exploit, dubbed FastUnlock , lives entirely inside software that ships with Windows. It requires no malware download, no credential theft and no memory corruption bug. It is a logic flaw, and according to former Microsoft researcher Abdelhamid Naceri it worked on every machine he tried.

The root of the problem sits between Narrator's redesigned interface and the lock screen's restricted account context. Microsoft gave the screen reader a new look but did not confine the refreshed UI to signed-in sessions.

Narrator can therefore be summoned while a machine is locked, where it runs under WsiAccount, the account the lock screen operates in. That context is supposed to be walled off from the running system. Instead, it hands an attacker a code execution path that operates outside the protections BitLocker and the sign-in flow are designed to enforce.

Triggering the chain takes physical access and little else. At the lock screen, the attacker selects "I forgot my PIN" (or password) and waits for the Microsoft account window asking how to reset the account. Pressing Win+U and opening Narrator at that point sends the screen reader to a background window it owns, one that never renders on screen and whose focus already rests on a "Next" button.

The attacker never needs to see it. Holding the Caps Lock key and steering with the arrow keys moves through the invisible window to a link labeled "Math reading settings." A press of Caps + Enter opens Narrator's settings, and from there a USB stick plugged into the machine is enough to reach File Explorer and the user's files.

Windows BitLocker exploit sparks messy feud between Microsoft and the researcher who exposed it

Windows will soon grade your PC's security, and apps like Battle.net get to see the score

Naceri said it took five minutes to go from finding the issue to breaching a fully encrypted, BitLocker-enabled machine running Windows 11 26H2 with the November 2026 patch installed. He blamed the bug on what he called "total negligence" on Microsoft's part.

The blast radius is narrower than the technique suggests however. There is no remote component, so the attacker must be physically at the keyboard and know the right combination of keys. The machine must also have at least one account linked to an online Microsoft account, because the reset flow that anchors the attack depends on it.

Devices running only local accounts are not affected. The attack also starts from a lock screen, which means it targets drives BitLocker has already unlocked at boot, as the default TPM-only setup does. A startup PIN would likely stop an attacker before the lock screen ever loads, though that has not been tested. For everyone else, Naceri's advice was blunt: "hold tight" until Microsoft ships a patch.

The disclosure fits a pattern that has made Naceri a recurring headache for his former employer. A security researcher based in Germany, he says Microsoft dismissed him in 2024, months before he could secure permanent EU residence, over a security incident he disputes. He sued for unfair termination, and insists the fight was never about bug bounties.

The public feud began in April , when he published BlueHammer, a Microsoft Defender exploit, without notice, saying the company's Security Response Center had ignored his reports and shut his account. Microsoft says it never received details beforehand. Since then he has released more than a dozen Windows zero-days under the names MSNightmare,…

items.title: Distro choice doesn’t matter anymore, and that’s why 2027 is the year Linux finally goes mainstream
items.content:
His love of PCs and their components was born out of trying to squeeze every ounce of performance out of the family computer. Tinkering with his own build at age 10 turned into building PCs for friends and family, fostering a passion that would ultimately take shape as a career path.

Besides being the first call for tech support for those close to him, Ty is a computer science student, with his focus being cloud computing and networking. He also competed in semi-pro Counter-Strike for 8 years, making him intimately familiar with everything to do with peripherals.

The first question that gets asked of a Windows user switching to Linux is which distro to install, and for many years, that was the correct one. It used to decide whether your Wi-Fi card would work or your games would launch first try, but now, it has lost a lot of its weight, and I think that's a good thing.

I've run many Linux distros on my desktop over the years, and I've settled on CachyOS for a multitude of reasons, but most of those are niche and specific to me. For someone who sees Ubuntu or Fedora and thinks it looks comfortable and welcoming, the best experience they can have on those distros can almost certainly match mine, and the only difference nowadays is defaults, most of which can be easily changed. That shift, more than any single distro getting better, is what gives 2027 a real chance of being the year Linux goes mainstream.

The parts you actually use are pretty much the same everywhere

Linux has most of what you need regardless of distro

Most new users will interact with parts of a Linux system that don't belong to a single distro. Flathub is a great example of this, and it works as a shared app store across distros, so the same build of Firefox, OBS, or Discord installs and behaves the same way on Fedora, Mint, or an Arch derivative.

For gamers, Steam goes a step further by adding Proton, a compatibility layer that hands a Windows game a standardized set of libraries regardless of the distro running underneath. If I go to run something like Cyberpunk 2077 on a machine running Ubuntu and then one running vanilla Arch, so long as both have the proper GPU drivers, they should run and behave the same way.

The host distro mostly just supplies the kernel, those graphics drivers, and core services like audio. On AMD and Intel hardware, even GPU drivers are the same upstream kernel and Mesa code everywhere; distros differ mainly in how recent a version they ship. Add in the fact that many distros today support either KDE Plasma or GNOME, and what a newcomer might think of as "the OS" is largely a shared experience across dozens of distros.

There are still day-to-day distro differences I've run into, but they're becoming less common as the years go by. For the Ubuntu 26.04 mini PC I run, Snap is the primary format for packages. It's the default for installing software, and the App Center lists Snap and Deb packages but leaves Flatpak out until you add it yourself. On CachyOS, which is the OS on my main workstation, you're pointed toward pacman and the wider Arch ecosystem, but you can easily install AppImages, too.

A lot of users probably won't be picking a distro

Perhaps the biggest shift we might see is that the choice of distro is made before the user enters the picture. Valve’s Steam Machine launched at the end of June 2026 running SteamOS, and anyone who buys one gets Linux without ever hearing or seeing the word "distribution."

SteamOS 3.8 extended that to self-built PCs with AMD graphics, which would help those who want to experience it outside their Steam hardware do so. The scale is still quite modest, and the level to which other OEMs sell machines with Linux as the installed OS is still dwarfed by their Windows sales, but it's trending upward.

Windows 10 is on the way out, for real this time

items.title: UK Court Forces Government to Confirm It Ordered Apple to Open iCloud Encryption
items.content:
The UK's Investigatory Powers Tribunal has confirmed that the UK government served Apple with a secret Technical Capability Notice. The order has been widely reported as demanding access to end-to-end encrypted iCloud data. The tribunal rejected the Home Office's argument that confirming the notice exists would damage national security.

The Home Office had followed its usual "neither confirm nor deny" policy on the case. The three judges pointed to extensive public reporting, statements by US officials and media briefings that they concluded the UK government had authorized.

A Technical Capability Notice is issued under the Investigatory Powers Act 2016. It forces companies to make technical changes that support the UK government's legal surveillance powers. The ruling confirms only that the notice exists. Its exact demands stay secret for now.

"Although there has been extensive media coverage and public statements about the existence of a technical capability notice, there has been no publication of its precise content," the judgment states.

The judges agreed that disclosing all the material would harm national security, but said not every detail has to stay secret, and that the exact boundaries cannot be set yet.

January 2025: the Home Office demands an iCloud backdoor, which becomes public in February 2025

February 2025: Apple removes Advanced Data Protection for UK users

August 2025: US officials say the UK agreed to drop its demand for access to Americans' encrypted data

October 2025: the UK reportedly replaces the original notice with a new order focused on British users

July 2026: Apple files a second legal challenge after its first was dismissed

first half of 2027: a full hearing is planned

Advanced Data Protection extends end to end encryption to more iCloud data, including backups, photos and notes. Only the user's trusted devices hold the keys, so Apple cannot decrypt that data for investigators.

Without it, the data is still encrypted, but Apple holds the keys and can hand content over in response to valid legal demands. Some categories stay end to end encrypted either way. The feature is still available in the US.

A government spokesperson defended the powers. "The right to privacy is crucial but it should not come at the expense of the safety of the British public," the spokesperson said, adding that the government "never has direct access to a company's communications systems or data" and that the notice "simply requires that they maintain the ability" to help police.

The proceedings also include a separate challenge to the notice regime from Liberty, Privacy International and two individuals. Apple has not publicly commented on the ruling.

items.title: Pill to treat pancreatic cancer hailed as 'biggest breakthrough in decades'
items.content:

A year after starting treatment, 76.6% of patients were alive; usually 40-45 % of patients given chemotherapy alone survive a year. Photograph: Jeff Moore/PA

Pill to treat pancreatic cancer hailed as ‘biggest breakthrough in decades’

Cancer undetectable for one in 12 patients in daraxonrasib trial, while nearly all participants’ tumours stopped growing

A pill that can shrink and potentially eliminate pancreas tumours is being hailed as the biggest breakthrough treatment for the cancer in decades.

In one in 12 of the patients given the drug, daraxonrasib , during a trial, the cancer became undetectable, and the tumours stopped growing in almost all of the 61 patients. The trial participants had recently been diagnosed with advanced pancreatic cancer that had spread to other parts of the body.

Though doctors have said the pill cannot yet be considered a cure, and they do not know how long it can keep the disease at bay, they have said it is encouraging news because it appears it will offer patients more time, even if it does not cause full remission.

‘The undruggable became druggable’: a gamechanging treatment for the world’s deadliest cancer – podcast

Half of all people diagnosed with pancreatic cancer die within three months, and only about 3% of patients survive for five years when the disease spreads to other organs. It has the lowest survival rate of all common cancers in the UK and has a similarly poor prognosis globally.

Patients were followed for a year and a half during the trial on average and some did not see the cancer return during this period. Longer studies will be conducted to see if any of the cancers can be put into remission. During the trial, tumours stopped growing in 90% of patients, just over 60% of patients had their tumours shrink or disappear, and for about 8% of patients tumours became undetectable on CT scans.

A year after starting treatment, 76.6% of patients were alive; usually 40-45% of patients given chemotherapy alone survive a year.

Dr Wungki Park, a gastrointestinal medical oncologist at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center in New York, who presented the findings, said “this is the closest to cure”, adding that he had never seen so many tumours disappear in patients whose cancer had spread.

He presented the findings at the EORTC-NCI-AACR Symposium on Molecular Targets and Cancer Therapeutics in Barcelona. “We are beginning to see not only a higher percentage of tumour response rates, but also deeper responses and a near doubling in the duration of disease control, which may eventually translate into longer survival,” he said.

FDA gives expedited approval to new groundbreaking pancreatic cancer drug

“The median follow-up is 18 months. Just imagine, in an average of 18 months your disease just disappears on the CT scan … that’s closest to complete remission … it’s incredible.”

Daraxonrasib is a KRAS inhibitor treatment, which works by locking on to and shutting off certain mutations found in most pancreatic cancers. These mutations drive tumour growth.

There are hopes the treatment could work for dozens of other cancers because they can have similar mutations.

Michelle Mitchell, Cancer Research UK’s chief executive, said more research was needed, but added: “This is the biggest leap forward we’ve seen in decades for pancreatic cancer patients and could offer real hope to people facing one of the deadliest and most difficult-to-treat cancers.

“These results raise the exciting possibility that this breakthrough could eventually pave the way for treating other cancers that carry Kras gene mutations. More trials are now needed before this treatment can be assessed for use on the NHS and despite this advance, pancreatic cancer survival is still very low.”

items.title: Zero-day exploit completely defeats default Windows 11 BitLocker protections
items.content:
A zero-day exploit circulating online allows people with physical access to a Windows 11 system to bypass default BitLocker protections and gain complete access to an encrypted drive within seconds.

The exploit, named YellowKey, was published earlier this week by a researcher who goes by the alias Nightmare-Eclipse. It reliably bypasses default Windows 11 deployments of BitLocker, the full-volume encryption protection Microsoft provides to make disk contents off-limits to anyone without the decryption key, which is stored in a secured piece of hardware known as a trusted platform module (TPM). BitLocker is a mandatory protection for many organizations, including those that contract with governments.

When one disk volume manipulates another

The core of the YellowKey exploit is a custom-made FsTx folder. Online documentation of this folder is hard to find. As explained later, the directory associated with the file fstx.dll appears to involve what Microsoft calls the transactional NTFS , which allows developers to have “transactional atomicity” for file operations in transactions with a single file, multiple files, or ones that span multiple sources.

The steps for carrying out the bypass are simple:

Copy the custom FsTx folder from the Nightmare-Eclipse exploit page to an NTFS- or FAT-formatted USB drive

Connect the USB drive to the BitLocker-protected device

Boot up the device and immediately press and hold down the [Ctrl] key

There are at least two ways to accomplish the third step. One way is to boot into Windows, hold down the [Shift] key, click on the power icon, and click restart. Another is to power on the device and restart it as soon as Windows starts booting.

In either case, a command (CMD.EXE) prompt appears. The prompt has full access to the entire drive contents, allowing an attacker to copy, modify, or delete them. In a normal Windows Recovery flow, the attacker would need to enter a BitLocker recovery key. Somehow, the YellowKey exploit bypasses this safeguard. Multiple researchers, including Kevin Beaumont and Will Dormann , have confirmed the exploit works as described here.

It’s unclear what in the custom FsTx folder causes the bypass. Dormann said that it appears to be related to Transactional NTFS, which itself uses command-log file system under the hood. Dormann further noted that by looking at the Windows fstx.dll, one will see code that explicitly looks for \System Volume Information\FsTx in the FsTxFindSessions() function.”

The contents of this FsTx directory used in the YellowKey exploit reveal no strings related to RecoverySimulation.ini. It does, however, show the files and paths \??\C:\Windows\win.ini and

\??\X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini, “where X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini is what controls what WinRE [Windows Recovery] does when it fires up.”

Dormann, who is a senior principal vulnerability analyst at Tharros Labs, continued:

But what’s intriguing to me is: Why can the presence a \System Volume Information\FsTx directory on one volume affect the contents of ANOTHER VOLUME when it’s replayed? 🤔

In a normal WinRE session, you have a X:\Windows\System32 directory that has a winpeshl.ini file in it:

However, with the YellowKey exploit, it looks like Transactional NTFS bits on a USB Drive are able to delete the winpeshl.ini file on ANOTHER DRIVE (X:). And we get a cmd.exe prompt, with bitlocker unlocked instead of the expected Windows Recovery environment. While the TPM-only Bitlocker bypass is indeed interesting, I think the buried lede here is that a \System Volume Information\FsTx directory on one volume has the ability to modify the contents of another volume when it is replayed. To me, this in and of itself sounds like a vulnerability.

A Microsoft representative declined to answer questions sent by email about the reported vulnerability other than to say the company is investigating.

items.title: Researcher plants 2m canaries into the AI supply chain. A privacy disaster surfaced: Test using prompts with unique, trackable secrets proves that data doesn’t stay private.
items.content:
Researchers planted 2 million digital tripwires in requests sent through a sprawling network of AI services to find out what happened to sensitive information entrusted to them. What they discovered was an ecosystem that leaked highly sensitive data like a sieve.

The exposure was found through an ingenious experiment designed to test if sensitive information can leak through the vast chain of widely used AI services and how that information is exploited when it does. Many of today’s AI apps use services such as OpenRouter or Vercel that act as brokers. These “AI routers,” sometimes also known as “AI gateways,” receive large numbers of prompts sent from AI app end users and route them to an available inference engine based on criteria such as the one charging the lowest price or being best suited for the given task. Instead of using Anthropic, OpenAI, or another big provider, the developer hires an AI router to find the most suitable model.

Security breaches, prompt theft, and privacy violations

To test for potential leakage, researcher HD Moore assembled a collection of Amazon Web Services access keys, functioning credentials tied to empty AWS accounts, passwords for services such as SSH, and unique URLs, DNS names, and private git repository references. None of the secrets had ever been used before, and he controlled the infrastructure that received any requests using the credentials. He then seeded each secret into exactly one prompt sent to a single provider. In the event any of the secrets were leaked, these “canaries”—so called because they resemble the role of that bird when taken into coal mines—would allow Moore to identify each link in the chain that was responsible.

The findings are striking. They included:

Evidence that at least three AI providers were compromised by attackers who used their access to siphon prompts they received

Multiple resellers in the inference marketplace that logged the prompts and somehow passed them along to people who used the credentials

Multiple cases of AI providers not following end-user privacy settings embedded into flags specifying terms such as Zero Data Retention (ZDR) or “no data collection”

“We sent nearly two million AI prompts containing unique, trackable secrets to AI providers, then watched where those secrets surfaced,” Moore, the chief research officer of security firm Dragos, wrote Thursday . “What we found revealed security breaches, prompt theft, and widespread failures to protect customer data.”

Although prompts are encrypted in transit, they are decrypted at each hop inside the large inference reseller network. The prompt is first sent to an AI router, which reads the plaintext in it to determine the most suitable inference providers to handle the request. Often, the prompt is then sent to a pool of available models, which sometimes run inside different hosting providers. Prompts can also pass from one AI router (such as Vercel) to another one (e.g., OpenRouter). Each one of these players is likely to log the prompt and store it for as long as its policies call for (if not indefinitely).

The most concerning finding was the breach of three separate hosting providers. The attackers who compromised one of the providers reused “a couple hundred” of the AWS keys. Moore wrote:

Each key was sent in exactly one request to one provider, all within a few short windows in late October, and every request we sent during those windows was stolen. Some of the stolen keys came from requests that the provider rejected before a model ever ran—this tells us that the attacker was copying requests at the provider’s front door, and not somewhere deeper in the inference stack. In the other two breaches, some of the stolen requests were marked as ZDR. A privacy flag doesn’t help when the attacker is already inside.

Parties tied to the hack of these three providers then tested each key, in some cases within hours of being seeded, to see what kind of resources it gave access to.…

items.content: 🚨 CVE-2026-133120 📢 Source: openjs 💣 CVSS Score: 9.1 (CRITICAL) 📡 Remotely Exploitable: False @fastify/express is a compatibility layer that lets Express middleware run inside the Fastify web framework. In versions before 4.0.10, the plugin passes Express a request URL that does not always match the path Fastify's router dispatched, so path-scoped Express middleware can be skipped while the route handler still runs. Several request forms trigger the mismatch, including percent-decoding that rewrites a backslash to a slash or double-decodes an encoded percent sign, and a request target that begins with an asterisk, so the middleware and the handler disagree on the path or on parameter and query values. An unauthenticated client can therefore reach a handler that an authentication, authorization, or rate-limiting middleware was meant to protect, with no special configuration required. The issue is fixed in @fastify/express 4.0.10, and users should upgrade to 4.0.10 or later. 📅 Published Date: 2026-11-21T17:08:07.453Z https://cvefeed.io/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-133120
